Params: <size=50>"Adelyde, there is no such thing as a miracle."\n"Hoping for something like that will only make you weak."</size>
"Adelyde, there is no such thing as a miracle."
"Hoping for something like that will only make you weak."
<size=50>"For thousands of years, \nhumanity trudged forward on nothing but their own hands and their own wits."</size>
"For thousands of years, humanity trudged forward on nothing but their own hands and their own wits."
<size=50>"Go <color=#ff4e4eff>win</color>."\n"Don't sit around waiting for a miracle to save you."</size>
"Don't sit around waiting for a miracle to save you."
The Helio family's simulated training ground allows no rest.
A rectangle of blocks forms the central track, piling at its end into a steel wall the color of old lead.
Above it all, the Helio crest presides, proud and untouchable.
From the shadowed curve of the ceiling, everything below seems as insignificant as crawling ants.
One of them is a child, bent beneath an enormous black cross, dragging herself forward one step at a time.
The cross cannon she carries, destined to become a formidable weapon in the future, now sits upon her young shoulders like a coffin too heavy for its bearer.
This time, I'm not going to lose.
The burden bows her frame, but never her spirit. She raises her face to the steel deity above and stares back without flinching.
Subject 23, Adelyde Helio. Lower your head.
The child doesn't budge. Her chin lifts even higher, and a flicker of fierceness enters her eyes, just a little too forced.
The voice is devoid of inflection, nearly mechanical. Only the faint trace of sternness that slips through reminds one that it belongs to a person, not the training ground's automated system.
The figure's posture is bolt-straight, hands locked behind the spine, facing the track with an air of unyielding discipline that mirrors the space around her.
The child turns toward her and forces the words out. Each syllable lands with the weight of the black cross pressing down on her shoulders.
Examiner, if I pass this test, will I finally be allowed to bring my mother home?
Helio does not break its word, but only if you earn it.
Adelyde looks ahead. Line after line of blue markers is etched on the gray data blocks. 12.3m, 23.4m, 31.9m... Each one is a distance she has already conquered.
But the farthest marker, a stark crimson line at 100m, is what Rusalka means by "earn it." A distance Adelyde has never reached.
Eyes fixed on the finish line, she strains to lift her foot. The massive cross shifts dangerously on her back, and for a moment her balance breaks, her frame tipping.
Keep your right foot back and your knees bent. Engage your core.
The child reacts instantly, just barely steadying herself. Beads of sweat roll down her temples.
I'll say this one last time. Lower your head.
Adelyde Helio, you don't have the strength to fight on willpower alone. Keep the wrong posture, and all you'll do is put unnecessary strain on your core and lower back.
The pride of the weak means nothing.
But if I succeed, I'm not weak. And if I win, then any posture should be allowed, right?
Words don't tip the scale of victory. I taught you that.
But an examiner is still obligated to answer a subject's questions.
If the subject succeeds, then yes, any posture and any method is permitted.
A triumphant smile tugs at Adelyde's mouth.
Over countless drills and tests, the observant child has long since noticed that some heirs would "operate" the cross.
Enter a specific sequence into the system, and the levitation system activates to adjust the load.
She has only ever caught a glimpse of the first half of that sequence from a distance, watching other heirs train. The second half has never been completed in her presence.
She has never learned it, but it's fine. She will crack it herself right now.
A glint of light flickers at the edge of her vision. Adelyde glances back in confusion, but the space behind her holds only emptiness.
It will happen this time, Examiner.
Adelyde dismisses the fleeting illusion and turns her attention back to Rusalka.
She grits her teeth and frees her right hand to pull up the operating system.
The moment her grip shifts, the cross tilts left, its full weight crushing down on her small left shoulder.
She does not stop. Her left shoulder bears the weight of a tilting world, her right hand fumbles through the air in trial after trial, and her feet drag forward inch by inch.
Rusalka watches in silence. She does not intervene or assist. She simply observes Adelyde with that same flat, unreadable gaze.
Florence Helio. The current model you are responsible for has been delayed again. This marks the fifth consecutive quarter that your overall evaluation has ranked at the bottom of the family.
Adelyde is still so little. She's been growing so fast lately. I really don't want to miss it...
The heir you are raising is also included in the assessment criteria. And her metrics also lag behind those of other heirs her age.
Her outstretched right hand gropes desperately in the air. Sweat drips into her eyes, and her vision blurs with a burning sting.
(It's just the last part. I'll try again... There has to be a pattern.)
Following the value assessment of Florence Helio, the conclusion is as follows:

Severe dissociative disorder triggered by high-stress environments. Condition is irreversible. She is no longer fit to perform her duties and holds no further potential for contributing to the family's interests.
Immediate transfer to a closed care facility is recommended.
That was the day they took her unconscious mother away.
Adelyde chased after them, her tiny fingers stretching forward, reaching for the hand that once guided her first steps.
She chased and prayed to gods that did not exist. She wanted her mother to get better. She did not want them to take her away.
But not a single adult stopped for her.
Another blue line falls behind her. This is uncharted ground now, a distance she has never touched. The weight is still crushing, but her feet keep moving.
Her fingers scrabble at the void, the motion frantic, as if she is gasping for air in a current that wants to pull her under.
And then her hand finds the last piece of the sequence.
——Auxiliary power system engaged, load factor reduced by 50%——
——Adelyde Helio, Class-D identity verification successful——\n——Auxiliary power system engaged, load factor reduced by 50%——
All at once, the crushing load lifts from her shoulders.
A message flickers across the interface, curt and unfeeling. Her clearance grants her just ten seconds of assistance.
And then she runs. She pours every ounce of herself into the sprint.
Markers fly by, distances she had only ever dreamed of. The weight is no longer crushing, and her legs carry her faster than they ever have.
For a moment, she feels like any other kid racing home from school, backpack bouncing, chasing the warmth of a door that waits open.
Easy now, Adelyde... Slow and steady.
It is one of the few hazy memories she has of her mother. Her mother bent before her, steadying her small hands and guiding her forward as she learned to walk.
Mommy's right here. So you don't need to be so fast, Adelyde.
Because just watching you grow up healthy and happy is already more than I could ever ask for.
Adelyde, there's something in this world called a "miracle."
It comes when a child needs it most and makes their wish come true.
<size=50>"If a miracle comes, will Mom get better?"</size>
"If a miracle comes, will Mom get better?"
But her mother never got better. The family sent her away to a care facility instead.
She has long since come to understand the Helio family's creed. The strong have a voice, and the weak are nothing.
(Then I'll prove it to all of you!)
No one responded to her voice. So she stopped praying and started acting. She stepped between the adults and her mother, a tiny barricade of stubborn will.
Her face tilted upward, eyes fixed on the Helio crest pinned to the person's uniform. She did not flinch.
I'll take good care of her, so please don't take her away.
Adelyde, there is no such thing as a miracle.
The child runs, gasping for breath, trying to argue back against the voice in her memory.
Her lungs burn with searing heat. Her throat is raw, stripped of the strength to cry out.
Adelyde, one of the heirs, lacks psychological maturity. Owing to Florence Helio's failure to provide proper upbringing, her overall performance remains notably inferior to that of her peers.
80m. Another marker blurs past beneath her feet. The red finish line ahead looks almost within reach.
The weight of reality comes crashing down on the child's back.
<color=#ff4e4eff>——Auxiliary power system offline, load factor restored——</color>
——Auxiliary power system offline, load factor restored——
She crumples to the floor, lungs clawing for air, her breaths shallow and torn. She was almost there. So close she could taste it.
That line marks everything she has ever wanted. A mother's warmth. A world's kindness. Things she still has left to prove.
And now it just sits there, that crimson line, laughing at how weak she is.
There it is again. That pale golden flash is caught this time in the instant Adelyde turns her head.
But in the blink of an eye, it is gone.
She does not have the strength to chase it, to name it, to shape it into a prayer. So her gaze returns to the red line ahead.
She has come a long way. Nearly fifty meters past her last record.
So no miracle came, after all.
The adult steps up beside her, not a word of praise to offer.
A broad cloak cuts the glare, leaving Rusalka's face lost in shadow. Her expression is unreadable.
Do you remember what we spoke about at the beginning?
Yes. I want to bring my mother home from the facility and take care of her myself. That's asking the family for a favor.
And in exchange, I must show the family that I have the strength they need to see.
She braces her palms against the floor and heaves upward, only to collapse as if an unseen hand is pressing her back down.
Her next attempt is met with a sudden release. Rusalka, with casual strength, lifts the cross from her shoulders and sets it on the nearby rack.
Learn from your mistakes, train harder, and prepare for the next test.
You're not mad? I just cracked the family's system.
The family only judges the outcome.
The provocation slides off her like water. Without so much as a shift in tone, she pronounces the final verdict.
And that outcome is you failed.
You overloaded your body. It's out of gas. At least 15 minutes before you can even think of moving. Forcing yourself up now will only put you back down.
Lie down on your side, and focus on getting your breath back.
She bends down briefly, scanning the child for any sign of injury. Satisfied, she drops a towel beside her and rises, already turning away.
The blue-gray tide recedes from the walls. One by one, the marker lines on the floor go dark. 10m. 20m. 80m. And finally, the red line at 100.
They vanish without a trace, as if no one had ever run here at all.
The simulation ends. The lights go out, and the training room falls into darkness.
Rusalka's back fades beyond the door. Only then does the child push herself up on trembling arms, crawl to her locker, and retrieve a little notebook.
<color=#ffffffff>When I feed her, I need to angle the spoon upward and make sure not to touch her teeth. I've been practicing a lot. I finally don't spill anymore.</color>
<color=#ffffffff>I have to turn her every two hours, even at night. I set an alarm. Now I wake up before it rings.</color>

<color=#ffffffff>The book says to keep talking to her, that a familiar voice might help. So I told her about my training. Then I started crying. They kicked me out. The nurse said she can't handle strong emotions.</color>
<color=#ffffffff>I'm not crying anymore. I've held it together for a long time now.</color>

<color=#ffffffff>If the weather's nice, they allow me to move her to the window so she gets sunlight. Mom hates the cold. She loves the sun and flowers. She used to grow so many in the backyard.</color>
<color=#ffffffff>I took her outside to get some sun. I've been taking care of all her plants. They will all bloom in spring. She'll see them when she comes home.</color>
<color=#ffffffff>Miss Rusalka says she can't do anything now. I said I don't care. Mom doesn't have to be strong when she's with me.</color>
<color=#ffffffff>That's why I have to be strong.</color>
She looks up and rehearses the motions from her little manual in the air. Feeding. Turning. Talking. Over and over.
Then, she adds a new line to the notebook, her hand pressing so firmly the ink smudges and the words tilt.
<color=#ffffffff>Load carry test, 80 meters. That's 50 meters farther than my best.</color>
By the time she's back, I'll have learned all of it.
I can't wait for her to come back. I have to be ready before then.
She flips through her notebook and starts figuring out the time she would need to run the remaining 20 meters.
With full load, 31.9 meters. With half load, 80 meters, still 20 meters short.
The simple fact is that 80 meters is her limit, given where her body is right now.
She could push until she vomits, run until the simulation cuts out from overuse. But no amount of willpower will make her bones grow overnight.
She presses her knees to the ground and shoves upward anyway. Maybe getting to her feet would be enough to prove the numbers wrong.
Her knees give out halfway up. She collapses hard, chin striking the floor, the sharp taste of blood flooding her mouth.
She does not get up again. Instead, she remains on the cold ground, moving her small arms through the caregiving motions, swaying with each repetition.

Across a continent of ten million square kilometers. In a family renowned throughout the Transatlantic Economic Community. At the heart of a five-hundred-square-meter training room, a child barely over a meter tall lies sprawled on the frigid floor, like a small wounded creature.
The weapons lining the walls watch her in silence, all staring down in silent disappointment.
"General Adelyde, under your command, we have suffered yet another defeat."
She speaks for the weapons on the walls, voicing their judgment until her chest grows tight. Then she begins to argue back against herself.
"I understand your anxiety, soldiers. But this campaign to reclaim her is far from over. One loss does not decide the war."
"But we have yet to win a single battle. Lady Florence's condition worsens with every passing day. You must lead us to save her from the dragon's lair, and soon."
"Our progress is still deeply concerning. As soldiers, we have the right to question your strategy."
The soldiers in her mind press forward with relentless accusation, and Adelyde cannot help but flinch.
The voice that comes out is hoarse, carrying no authority at all. Adelyde quickly stops herself and switches to a more serious tone.
"Soldiers, you must have faith in my judgment. Every move I have made is the optimal choice for the big picture."
"I am a general, not a sorcerer. I cannot bend time forward or backward."
"That's no excuse for our failure today."
The words hit too hard. Adelyde slaps her hands over her ears.
"General, we have failed the load carry campaign one hundred and one times in a row. At this pace, will we ever win?"
"Will the 'miracle' you keep mentioning ever arrive?"
She closes her eyes, hugs the notebook to her chest, and curls herself into a tight ball.
Just say something kind to me... Don't keep asking questions I don't have answers to.
Adelyde does not like the sight of herself failing. She does not like talking to herself. She does not like the dark, or Rusalka's silence, or the family taking her mother away, or empty rooms.
She does not like "miracles" either, because they never seem to come.
A faint light catches at the edge of her vision. Adelyde opens her eyes. There, in the corner, a small lamp flickers on.
The rest of the training ground has sunk into cold, disapproving shadow. Only this one remains, a small sentinel standing guard over her.
It glows alone, a fragile light holding back the weight of a world's darkness.
Poor little thing. Just like me.
Adelyde murmurs softly, a warm smile tugging at the corners of her mouth.
And then, a pale golden light spills across the floor beneath the lamp. It looks exactly like the light she had glimpsed before.
A dimly glowing silhouette stands in the entrance, cast in pale gray.
She snatches the pistol at her side and levels it at the figure, switching off the safety and chambering a round in one fluid motion.
All the tension she had released floods back in a second. Her tone turns so icy that she surprises herself.
Five meters at most. A static target. She is confident she could drop it in one shot. Yet the silhouette remains planted at the door, refusing to retreat.
Seeing that she has not intimidated the intruder, Adelyde decides to press for more.
Talk. How did you get in here? The family armory requires five levels of clearance. It's impossible to get through without all of them.
And if you got through that door, you'd have to get past Rusalka first.
...No. That's impossible. No one can beat Rusalka.
She shakes her head, dismissing the thought.
The figure's lips part, and fragmented syllables slip out, fumbling to form her name.
The syllables tumble out in clumsy fragments, but it's plain that the figure is putting every ounce of effort into reaching her.
You mean I did... really well?
Keep your chin up... keep moving...
Who are you really? I don't need your pity.
Her teeth lock together, and a tremor runs through her frame. She feels caught in a massive current, spinning and helpless, every emotion she has refusing to stay buried. She feels fragile.
And she's a child who hates to appear fragile. So she tries to arm herself with sharper words.
Before any answer can come, the pale gray figure begins to flicker, its glow breaking apart into snowy static.
Then, the figure is caught in a current of light, powerless to resist.
Hey, what's happening? You haven't answered me—
With each word more broken than the last, Adelyde feels it coming. The figure is about to leave. She ignores the spinning world, forces herself up, and lunges toward it.
She only grabs at empty air. Through the crushing disappointment, she strains to read the phantom's lips one last time before it fades completely.
The pale gray figure is gone.
Only one light remains, like a candle left behind, proof that the figure was ever there at all.
You're up. Didn't I tell you to stay down for fifteen minutes?
There's a lamp on here. Was it you?
No... I don't know how it's turned on.
Maybe it saw you were afraid of the dark.
Rusalka offers a teasing remark, but then she notices Adelyde's expression has gone completely still.
When I got back, you were shouting at the door.
I was tired... I think I was seeing things.
Sounds like you really ran yourself ragged.
The child does not like being made fun of. Her head twists aside, her expression pinched with embarrassment.
Why are you here? Training is over.
The Erhorn family's head and the Science Council's Chief Technician want to meet the Helio heirs. Clean yourself up. We're leaving soon.
Here. A training biscuit. Eat it and get your strength back.
Adelyde murmurs a subdued acknowledgment, her small hand reaching out to accept the compressed biscuit.
—Or you can have this strawberry cake made with the best cream. Which one do you want?
Adelyde freezes, as if she cannot quite believe what she just heard.
That's the chef's cake for you, isn't it? You love strawberries.
Twenty meters short is still twenty meters short. Even 0.1 meters is a failure. That doesn't change.
But you pushed yourself hard, Adelyde. That matters.
The heavy walnut wood door closes with a low groan, muffling the din of the banquet hall beyond. In an instant, the sprawling room is wrapped in quiet.
The Helio household sees a constant stream of associates and dignitaries, so dedicated reception chambers are always kept prepared.
The room Adelyde now sits in has gone over a thousand days without receiving a single guest. Yet not a speck of dust has settled on it. This room was kept for two special visitors in particular.
Let us now welcome our two esteemed guests, Mr. Dominik and Mr. Erhorn, to address the gathering.
The first stands as the Science Council's Chief Technician and a guiding figure of humanity. The second is a prodigy without equal in the Erhorn lineage, overseeing all research into the M.I.N.D.
Just then, a familiar pale-gold flicker catches the corner of Adelyde's eye. She watches, astonished, as the gray figure from her "illusion" steps into the room.
Before she can even process what she is seeing, the leader of humanity begins his address from behind the dark brown writing desk.
Good evening, young ladies and gentlemen. We stand at the crossroads of an age defined by change, and by challenge.

I trust you've learned from your elders and your history books when humanity discovered new continents, the year we first set foot on the moon, and how long it took for the drifting Dawn-III to leave the galaxy it calls home.
All those facts and figures we now take for granted were once built upon failure and mystery beyond reckoning.
And today, the mystery we face is our own planet. The ocean that has given us life, and now demands our care.
This is a planetary-scale undertaking to command the currents along the Atlantic's backbone, to hold the climate in balance, and to ensure that humanity will never again succumb to an ice age.
At the very heart of the Atlantic's fiercest waters, we have built a current hydrodynamic energy system.
A ring forged above the waves, gazing skyward on humanity's behalf. We named it the Atlantic Eye.
Adelyde murmurs the name under her breath. She does not yet know what it signifies, and before she can even begin to make sense of it, Dominik has already moved on.
Young people, you are the future of the Transatlantic Economic Community. And the brilliance you carry is exactly what the Atlantic Eye seeks.
In return, the Atlantic Eye will offer you everything it has.
The leader of humanity pauses and casts a glance at the colleague beside him. The other picks up the thread without missing a beat.
You will be part of the Atlantic Eye's Watcher program, a training initiative for the next generation of core technicians, designed to cultivate excellence at the highest levels.
You will not be idle spectators, watching from the sidelines as history is written by others.

If you have the will and the talent, you will have direct access to the most advanced experiments and engineering projects—from drawing board to blueprint, from model to reality, backed by the finest resources the Transatlantic Economic Community and the wider world can provide.
You will pour your minds into the very foundation of this work, its bones, its blood, the miracle at its heart. And in doing so, you will help shape the eternity of humanity itself.

A wave of barely suppressed gasps ripples through the audience. These children know what the two men have achieved together, and the radiant future they speak of feels close enough to be almost within reach.
We have selected the first pilot members today. And as the program expands, many more of you will have your chance.
The names are... Auguste Helio, Rene Helio...
He proceeds down the roster until he arrives at the very last one.
The evening is ordinary, but the moment is not. Young Adelyde stands surrounded by the Helio heirs, planted at a turning point in the river of destiny.
She does not yet see the towering waves that will come, nor the scale of the pain and glory that await her at the Atlantic Eye.
A thousand paths seem open to her. In truth, she holds none.
So she must reach for this great future with both hands.
Trembling with barely contained excitement, Adelyde signs the training program's consent form.
The young heirs of the Helio family disperse, and the enormous chamber returns to its heavy quiet.
If you took the closing words for every address, I'd save a great deal of effort trying to persuade people.
In the art of rhetoric, you've always had the upper hand.
Don't drag me into more meetings with trivial minds. Family politics aside, I've got no patience for them.
My thoughts are needed elsewhere, on work that actually matters. And frankly, I'd say the same to you. Spend less time outside the lab.
The leader of humanity lets out a soft laugh and raises his hands in mock surrender. He steps closer to his colleague, peering at the terminal screen that has captured the other's full attention.
Have you settled on the final candidate from Spelmin?
Their father, Tavis, has already laid out a clear direction. I'll defer to his judgment.
Though, the other one's evaluation report... Forget it. It's your decision.
Dominik adds the name "Helentine Spelmin" to the next roster for the Atlantic Eye's training program.
Young Adelyde has no way of knowing how many people she will stand beside, or how many she will never get the chance to meet.
The leader of humanity finalizes the list, then lifts his gaze. He holds it somewhere beside the door, as though a phantom lingers there.
Hm? What are you staring at?
Dominik glances down at the terminal, and a single number shifts before his eyes.
Were anyone watching closely, they would notice that his famously steady gaze now holds a flicker of something else. Sheer, profound shock.
(You come from the future... where Ananke is already active?)
Don't zone out on me now. There's an experiment at the Atlantic Eye tonight, and we're both expected.
Right... Let's go. There's still a great deal to do.
The brief drifting journey ends, and the current sweeps you back into this desolate emptiness once more.
You hold out your hands. Your fingertips are still translucent, golden light threading through the lines of your palms.
(Start with what you've learned so far)
It took almost the entire night to establish the pathway, while you watched Adelyde fight through every hour of it. And in the end, you had only a moment to push a few broken words through.
You cannot touch anything. You cannot change anything. You cannot even choose when or where you appear.
The connection with Adelyde was not something you initiated yourself. It felt more like being drawn in by some unseen force.
(Maybe the same person who sent those cryptic messages)
There is no way to confirm your guess.
The only lead may be the golden strings of light before you. According to Aristo, these are Ytterbium-174 rays released by Ananke.
And yet the very thing it exists to protect, the Atlantic Eye itself, has only just been built.
Adelyde, still a child, now holds a ticket inside. If you can keep this connection alive, you might enter the Atlantic Eye with her and uncover the truth of Ananke's design.
Meanwhile, more questions surge forward, one after another.
Dominik. You have finally seen him with your own eyes.
The man who shaped humanity's future left no record of his own likeness. His face could only be guessed at through his works. Almost no one had seen him in person.

A single word from behind that desk, and the murmuring hall fell silent. He spoke without raising his voice, yet a project that risked the fate of the planet felt, in his mouth, like a foregone conclusion.
But as the room dispersed, the glance he cast toward the door, toward where you stood hidden, betrayed something beneath that unshakeable calm. It was a shadow that would not lift.
Still no way to find the answers.
And then there was the man at Dominik's side. Arius Erhorn.

The same man who, in your era, would tear down the dam to piece together a complete "Understanding" Sefirah. Tonight, he is only a proud speaker, painting a golden tomorrow for the young heirs, speaking for the friend beside him.
(A fellow creator to an obsessed predator... what happened?)
The words Rusalka spoke to you before she hurled you into the water come back to you now, carrying a chill that you cannot name.
Help us bring back the method to unravel the golden threads. Arius trusts you won't disappoint.
(Was my fall into this era part of his plan, too?)
(What does he want me to accomplish in the past for him?)
"It's where that child is headed. Guide her along the way."
"It's where that child is headed. Guide her along the way."
Golden words flash into being, then vanish just as quickly, as though drawn back into the depths by some greater force.
The boundless sea of time falls silent once more. In its stillness, a single beacon remains: the small figure from memory, bearing a cross on her back.
